title: Generative Representation Learning on Hyper-relational Knowledge Graphs via Masked Discrete Diffusion
one_liner: KREPE generates missing facts in knowledge graphs by treating each fact as a discrete diffusion problem, learning what hidden entities and relationships should be based on incomplete clues.
lead: A knowledge graph stores facts about the world as triples: (person, works-at, company). Most link-prediction methods assume two parts of the triple are known and only guess the third. But in the real world, you might know only the person, or have a fact with multiple blanks to fill, or need to generate entirely new facts. KREPE tackles this harder problem by learning to generate all missing pieces of a fact at once, using a method called masked discrete diffusion.

problem.h2: Why link prediction is too narrow
paras: A knowledge graph is a database of facts, each written as a triple: (subject, relation, object). For example, (Alice, works-at, Google), (Gold, atomic-number, 79). The standard task is link prediction: given two parts of the triple, guess the third. So if you know Alice and works-at, you predict Google.

But real-world facts often have multiple missing pieces. You might see (?, works-at, Google) and need to generate all matching employees. Or (Alice, ?, Google) to infer the relationship. Or (?, ?, ?) to generate facts from scratch. The old methods break because they were built assuming only one blank.

Hyper-relational knowledge graphs are even more complex: each fact can have additional context attributes (time, location, confidence) attached to it. Filling in just one missing piece while ignoring the rest leaves incomplete, unrealistic facts.

callout.html: Generate valid facts with multiple or all components missing simultaneously, respecting the graph's global structure and relationships.

panels.title: 1. Knowledge graph: dense triples

panels.caption: One blank only. Many real queries have multiple blanks.

steps.text: Take the partially masked fact. For blanks, use a placeholder.
Fill blanks with noise. This is the starting point for refinement.
Send information along graph edges: entities and relations pass signals to neighbors.
Use those signals to gradually replace noise with more probable entities and relations.
After many refinement steps, masked values have been replaced with valid fact components.

paras: KREPE changes what the model generates. Instead of outputting one missing entity or relation, it outputs complete, multi-component facts even when multiple pieces are unknown. It learns a generative distribution (a probability model) over all valid fact components conditioned on the known pieces and the entire graph structure.

hidden.name: conditional probability of each unknown piece
paras: KREPE learns a probability distribution: given some known parts of a fact and the global graph, what is the probability of each possible entity or relation for each unknown slot? For example, if we know (Alice, works-at, ?) the model learns the probability that Google, Facebook, Amazon, etc. fill the blank, incorporating the fact that Alice likely works at companies that have hired other people in the graph.

The paper estimates this distribution using a technique called discrete diffusion: it runs an iterative refinement process that gradually moves from random guesses toward real, valid fact components. At each step, the refinement uses contextual signals from the graph—nearby facts, entity types, relation patterns—to update probabilities for each blank. The process operates on discrete choices (which entity? which relation?) rather than continuous numbers.

heat.caption: Darker means higher probability. Highlights mark entities/relations chosen.

reads.html: The model learns to estimate: if I know some pieces of a fact and see the surrounding graph, how likely is each possible completion?
KREPE models the conditional distribution via masked discrete diffusion, using intra-fact message passing and inter-fact context aggregation to condition on both local and global structure.

paras: Generating an unseen fact is hard because you must satisfy many constraints at once: the entities must be real and of the right type, the relations must connect plausibly, and the entire triple must fit the graph's patterns. Trying to guess all blanks at once from scratch fails because there are too many bad combinations.

KREPE breaks this into small steps. It starts with random guesses and refines them iteratively. At each refinement step, the model sends information through the graph: each entity tells its neighbors what relations point to it, each relation broadcasts what entity types it typically links. Known pieces of the query act as anchors, biasing the refinement toward consistent completions. After many refinement steps, the random guesses have been gradually replaced with values that satisfy both the local query constraints and the global graph structure.

This works because each refinement step is much simpler than the full generation problem. Instead of guessing all blanks at once, the model simply asks: given what we know so far, which entities or relations are more likely here? The iterative process accumulates these local decisions into a coherent global fact.

stages.s: Partially masked fact, known fact context, graph edges
Encode known parts as numbers for computation
Message pass: entities and relations exchange signals
Update probabilities for each blank using signals plus known anchors
Completed fact with high-probability entities and relations

math.words: probability score for entity e in slot i equals: (local signal from known fact parts) plus (global signal from graph neighbors) plus (alignment score between entity type and expected role), normalized to sum to 1 across all possible entities
math.equation: P(e_i | known, graph) = exp(score_local(known_i) + score_global(neighbors_i) + score_type(e)) / Z
symbols: the entity filling the i-th blank
the known pieces of the fact
signal from the known query parts, e.g., does e match the known relation type?
entities and relations connected to this blank by graph edges
how often does e appear in those neighbors' facts?
is e the right entity type for this role?
normalization constant so probabilities sum to 1

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Query: (Alice, works-at, ?). Known parts score 2.0. Graph neighbors (employees at Google) add score 1.5. Entity type (company) adds 0.8.
Candidate: Google. Total unnormalized score: exp(2.0 + 1.5 + 0.8) = exp(4.3) ≈ 73.7.
Candidate: Alice (wrong type). Total: exp(2.0 + 0.1 + 0.0) = exp(2.1) ≈ 8.2.
Candidate: TechCorp (less common, fewer neighbors). Total: exp(2.0 + 0.3 + 0.8) = exp(3.1) ≈ 22.3.
Normalize: P(Google) = 73.7 / (73.7 + 8.2 + 22.3) ≈ 0.73. Google is most likely.

math.note: Over many refinement iterations, these local probability updates propagate through the graph, gradually steering random noise toward valid, unseen facts.

charts.title: Link prediction only: one blank at a time
charts.note: Old methods fail when multiple pieces are missing. They were built for one-blank problems only.

charts.title: KREPE: handles any masking pattern
charts.note: Iterative diffusion refines all unknowns simultaneously, using graph structure to guide each step.

items.html: If you stop the diffusion early, masks are still partially noisy. The refinement process needs enough iterations to propagate signals from known anchors through the graph. Too few steps means incompletely refined blanks.

If a blank entity is far from any known pieces in the graph, the messages traveling through edges will dilute. The refinement may revert to random guesses for isolated slots. Link prediction works best on densely connected graphs.

If the correct completion is an uncommon entity, the type score and global neighbor scores may both be low. The model could mislabel a blank with a common entity instead. Rare facts are harder to generate.
Set refinement steps high enough, ensure query-relevant graph neighborhoods are dense, and handle rare entities with class balancing or separate training objectives.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small knowledge graph: 20 entities (companies, people, cities) and 5 relation types (works-at, located-in, founder-of, employee-count, established-year). Create 50 training facts. Train KREPE with 30 refinement steps. Then test three scenarios: fill one blank (old link prediction), fill two blanks (a new capability), fill zero blanks (generate a fact the model has never seen). Measure: how many generated facts are valid (correct entity types, realistic relation) and how many are unseen (not in the training set)?
demo.metric_eq: validity = (facts with correct types and sensible relations) / (total generated facts); unseen_rate = (facts not in training set) / (total valid facts)
demo.closing: The demo must show that KREPE generates unseen, type-correct facts with multiple blanks, and that vanilla link prediction fails or produces gibberish when forced to fill multiple slots.
